claim: Microstimulation in the somatosensory cortex can evoke artificial tactile percepts.
source: Microstimulation in the somatosensory cortex can evoke artificial tactile percepts and can be incorporated into bidirectional brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) to restore function after injury or disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known capability of microstimulation, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Microstimulation can be incorporated into bidirectional brain-computer interfaces to restore function after injury or disease.
source: Microstimulation in the somatosensory cortex can evoke artificial tactile percepts and can be incorporated into bidirectional brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) to restore function after injury or disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an application of microstimulation technology.

claim: Increasing the amplitude increased the perceived intensity on all tested electrodes.
source: Increasing the amplitude and train duration increased the perceived intensity on all tested electrodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing the train duration increased the perceived intensity on all tested electrodes.
source: Increasing the amplitude and train duration increased the perceived intensity on all tested electrodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing the frequency evoked more intense percepts on some electrodes.
source: Surprisingly, we found that increasing the frequency evoked more intense percepts on some electrodes but evoked less-intense percepts on other electrodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Increasing the frequency evoked less-intense percepts on other electrodes.
source: Surprisingly, we found that increasing the frequency evoked more intense percepts on some electrodes but evoked less-intense percepts on other electrodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Different frequency-intensity relationships were divided into three groups.
source: These different frequency–intensity relationships were divided into three groups, which also evoked distinct percept qualities at different stimulus frequencies.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis using k-means clustering, as described in the methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The three frequency-intensity groups evoked distinct percept qualities at different stimulus frequencies.
source: These different frequency–intensity relationships were divided into three groups, which also evoked distinct percept qualities at different stimulus frequencies.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neighboring electrode sites were more likely to belong to the same group.
source: Neighboring electrode sites were more likely to belong to the same group.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's spatial analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4 and statistical analysis using LISA.

claim: Stimulation frequency directly controls tactile perception.
source: These results support the idea that stimulation frequency directly controls tactile perception and that these different percepts may be related to the organization of somatosensory cortex, which will facilitate principled development of stimulation strategies for bidirectional BCIs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, based on the observed effects of frequency on intensity and quality.

claim: Different percepts may be related to the organization of somatosensory cortex.
source: These results support the idea that stimulation frequency directly controls tactile perception and that these different percepts may be related to the organization of somatosensory cortex, which will facilitate principled development of stimulation strategies for bidirectional BCIs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, particularly the spatial clustering of electrode groups.

claim: Bidirectional brain-computer interfaces can restore lost function to people living with damage to the brain, spine, and limbs.
source: Bidirectional brain–computer interfaces (BCI) can restore lost function to people living with damage to the brain, spine, and limbs (Collinger et al., 2018; Fetz, 2015; Flesher et al., 2021; Hughes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: BCI users can control an end effector using neural activity recorded from motor cortex.
source: BCI users can control an end effector using neural activity recorded from motor cortex and receive sensory feedback through intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) in somatosensory cortex (Flesher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: BCI users can receive sensory feedback through intracortical microstimulation in somatosensory cortex.
source: BCI users can control an end effector using neural activity recorded from motor cortex and receive sensory feedback through intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) in somatosensory cortex (Flesher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The behavioral effects of ICMS in somatosensory cortex have been studied in detail in non-human primates.
source: The behavioral effects of ICMS in somatosensory cortex have been studied in detail in non-human primates (NHPs) (Dadarlat et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015a; Kim et al., 2015b; Romo et al., 2000; Romo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in non-human primates.

claim: Animals are limited in their ability to perform certain psychophysical tasks.
source: However, animals are limited in their ability to perform certain psychophysical tasks.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of animal research, based on established knowledge.

claim: NHPs can learn to discriminate between two or more stimuli.
source: NHPs can learn to discriminate between two or more stimuli, and their ability to perform these tasks can provide insight into how stimulus parameters affect sensory perception.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about non-human primate capabilities in behavioral experiments.

claim: NHPs cannot describe the qualitative nature of sensory percepts.
source: However, they can never describe the qualitative nature of the sensory percepts, nor can they be trained to perform more complex psychophysical tasks such as magnitude estimation.
evidence: This is a statement about the inherent limitations of animal research, based on established knowledge.

claim: NHPs cannot be trained to perform complex psychophysical tasks such as magnitude estimation.
source: However, they can never describe the qualitative nature of the sensory percepts, nor can they be trained to perform more complex psychophysical tasks such as magnitude estimation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of animal research, based on established knowledge.

claim: Limited work has been conducted in humans using ICMS of somatosensory cortex to restore sensation.
source: Limited work has been conducted in humans using ICMS of somatosensory cortex to restore sensation (Armenta Salas et al., 2018; Fifer et al., 2020; Flesher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: ICMS can evoke tactile sensations that are perceived to originate from the hands.
source: From these studies we know that ICMS can evoke tactile sensations that are perceived to originate from the hands (Fifer et al., 2020; Flesher et al., 2016) and arms (Armenta Salas et al., 2018) and that the stimulation locations in the cortex that elicit these percepts agree with known cortical somatotopy (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: ICMS can evoke tactile sensations that are perceived to originate from the arms.
source: From these studies we know that ICMS can evoke tactile sensations that are perceived to originate from the hands (Fifer et al., 2020; Flesher et al., 2016) and arms (Armenta Salas et al., 2018) and that the stimulation locations in the cortex that elicit these percepts agree with known cortical somatotopy (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: The stimulation locations in the cortex that elicit percepts agree with known cortical somatotopy.
source: From these studies we know that ICMS can evoke tactile sensations that are perceived to originate from the hands (Fifer et al., 2020; Flesher et al., 2016) and arms (Armenta Salas et al., 2018) and that the stimulation locations in the cortex that elicit these percepts agree with known cortical somatotopy (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies and classical work on somatotopy.

claim: Participants reported naturalistic sensations such as 'pressure' and 'touch'.
source: Participants reported naturalistic sensations such as 'pressure' and 'touch' (Flesher et al., 2016) as well as 'squeeze' and 'tap' (Armenta Salas et al., 2018), but the quality and naturalness varied between stimulated electrodes within each participant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: Participants reported naturalistic sensations such as 'squeeze' and 'tap'.
source: Participants reported naturalistic sensations such as 'pressure' and 'touch' (Flesher et al., 2016) as well as 'squeeze' and 'tap' (Armenta Salas et al., 2018), but the quality and naturalness varied between stimulated electrodes within each participant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: The quality and naturalness of sensations varied between stimulated electrodes within each participant.
source: Participants reported naturalistic sensations such as 'pressure' and 'touch' (Flesher et al., 2016) as well as 'squeeze' and 'tap' (Armenta Salas et al., 2018), but the quality and naturalness varied between stimulated electrodes within each participant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: All studies found that increasing the stimulus current amplitude consistently increased the perceived intensity of the tactile percepts.
source: Additionally, all studies found that increasing the stimulus current amplitude consistently increased the perceived intensity of the tactile percepts.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous human studies, supported by the context of citations.

claim: Low frequencies may require higher amplitudes to evoke a detectable percept.
source: The effect of stimulus pulse frequency has been less studied, although low frequencies may require higher amplitudes to evoke a detectable percept (Armenta Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous human study.

claim: Increasing the stimulation amplitude increased percept intensity in thalamic stimulation studies.
source: Similar to ICMS, increasing the stimulation amplitude increased percept intensity (Dostrovsky et al., 1993; Swan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous thalamic stimulation studies.

claim: In some cases high-frequency stimulation (333 Hz) evoked the most natural percepts in thalamic stimulation.
source: In some cases high-frequency stimulation (333 Hz) evoked the most natural percepts (Heming et al., 2010), while in others it evoked primarily paresthesias and low-frequencies produced "tapping" sensations (Dostrovsky et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous thalamic stimulation studies.

claim: In some thalamic stimulation cases, high-frequency stimulation evoked primarily paresthesias and low-frequencies produced 'tapping' sensations.
source: In some cases high-frequency stimulation (333 Hz) evoked the most natural percepts (Heming et al., 2010), while in others it evoked primarily paresthesias and low-frequencies produced "tapping" sensations (Dostrovsky et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous thalamic stimulation studies.

claim: Burst stimulation evoked more natural percepts than tonic stimulation in thalamic stimulation.
source: In other cases burst stimulation evoked more natural percepts than tonic stimulation (Willsey et al., 2020) and two-pulse bursts evoked less natural sensations (Swan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous thalamic stimulation studies.

claim: Two-pulse bursts evoked less natural sensations in thalamic stimulation.
source: In other cases burst stimulation evoked more natural percepts than tonic stimulation (Willsey et al., 2020) and two-pulse bursts evoked less natural sensations (Swan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous thalamic stimulation studies.

claim: Increasing the pulse frequency of ICMS reduced the current amplitude required to evoke a detectable percept in NHPs.
source: Increasing the pulse frequency of ICMS reduced the current amplitude required to evoke a detectable percept in NHPs (Kim et al., 2015a; Romo et al., 2000; Romo et al., 1998) and rats (Butovas and Schwarz, 2007; Semprini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: Increasing the pulse frequency of ICMS reduced the current amplitude required to evoke a detectable percept in rats.
source: Increasing the pulse frequency of ICMS reduced the current amplitude required to evoke a detectable percept in NHPs (Kim et al., 2015a; Romo et al., 2000; Romo et al., 1998) and rats (Butovas and Schwarz, 2007; Semprini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: In a frequency discrimination task, increasing amplitude biased NHPs toward selecting stimulus trains as having higher frequencies.
source: Additionally, in a frequency discrimination task, increasing amplitude biased NHPs (Callier et al., 2020) and rats (Fridman et al., 2010) toward selecting stimulus trains as having higher frequencies, providing further evidence that increasing pulse frequency increases perceived intensity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: In a frequency discrimination task, increasing amplitude biased rats toward selecting stimulus trains as having higher frequencies.
source: Additionally, in a frequency discrimination task, increasing amplitude biased NHPs (Callier et al., 2020) and rats (Fridman et al., 2010) toward selecting stimulus trains as having higher frequencies, providing further evidence that increasing pulse frequency increases perceived intensity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: Perceived intensity increases as stimulation amplitude and frequency are increased in human peripheral nerves.
source: Perceived intensity also increases as stimulation amplitude and frequency are increased in human peripheral nerves (Graczyk et al., 2016) and human visual cortex (Schmidt et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: Perceived intensity increases as stimulation amplitude and frequency are increased in human visual cortex.
source: Perceived intensity also increases as stimulation amplitude and frequency are increased in human peripheral nerves (Graczyk et al., 2016) and human visual cortex (Schmidt et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: Perceived intensity increased with increasing vibration frequency in able-bodied human participants using tactile input to the hand.
source: This is also true for mechanical stimuli where perceived intensity increased with increasing vibration frequency in able-bodied human participants using tactile input to the hand (Hollins and Roy, 1996; Muniak et al., 2007; Verrillo et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human psychophysics studies.

claim: Two participants (P2 and P3) with cervical spinal cord injuries had microelectrode arrays implanted into the motor and somatosensory cortices.
source: In ongoing experiments, we implanted microelectrode arrays into the motor and somatosensory cortices of two participants (referred to as P2 and P3) with cervical spinal cord injuries to evaluate the safety and efficacy of bidirectional BCIs and to study sensorimotor control in humans.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants and experimental setup.

claim: In P2, ICMS of somatosensory cortex evoked tactile percepts that felt like they originated from the paralyzed hand.
source: In P2, ICMS of somatosensory cortex evoked tactile percepts that felt like they originated from the paralyzed hand (Flesher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work with this participant.

claim: The percepts evoked in P2 varied considerably, from more natural sensations to less natural sensations.
source: However, the percepts themselves varied considerably, from more natural sensations, such as touch and pressure, to less natural sensations, such as vibration and tingle.
evidence: This is a description of observations from the participant, based on previous work.

claim: Modulated sensory feedback is crucial for object interaction.
source: The ability to control perceived intensity in a bidirectional BCI will be essential, as modulated sensory feedback is crucial for object interaction (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Nowak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on sensorimotor control.

claim: Conveying grip force requires the ability to modulate the perceived intensity of a stimulus.
source: While grasp contact could be relayed by simple on–off stimulation, conveying grip force, which is essential for grasp stability, efficiency, and precision (Godfrey et al., 2016; Nowak et al., 2004; Nowak and Hermsdörfer, 2006), requires the ability to modulate the perceived intensity of a stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the importance of grip force feedback, supported by citations.

claim: Grip force is essential for grasp stability, efficiency, and precision.
source: While grasp contact could be relayed by simple on–off stimulation, conveying grip force, which is essential for grasp stability, efficiency, and precision (Godfrey et al., 2016; Nowak et al., 2004; Nowak and Hermsdörfer, 2006), requires the ability to modulate the perceived intensity of a stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on motor control.

claim: The relationship between stimulus frequency and perceived intensity was electrode dependent.
source: However, the relationship between stimulus frequency and perceived intensity was electrode dependent (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: On some electrodes, percept intensity increased with stimulus pulse frequency.
source: On some electrodes, percept intensity increased with stimulus pulse frequency (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On over half of the tested electrodes, stimulus trains with low pulse frequencies (20–100 Hz) were perceived as being the most intense and the intensity decreased as the stimulus pulse frequency increased.
source: However, on over half of the tested electrodes, the opposite effect occurred; stimulus trains with low pulse frequencies (20–100 Hz) were perceived as being the most intense and the intensity decreased as the stimulus pulse frequency increased (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: K-means clustering was used to separate electrodes into three categories based on the reported percept intensity at 20, 100, and 300 Hz.
source: We used k-means clustering to separate electrodes into three categories based on the reported percept intensity at 20, 100, and 300 Hz (Figure 1—figure supplement 2): electrodes with the highest intensity response at 20 Hz (Figure 2A), electrodes with the highest intensity responses at 100 Hz (Figure 2B), and electrodes with the highest intensity response at 300 Hz (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used in the study.

claim: The three electrode groups are referred to as high-frequency preferring (HFP), intermediate-frequency preferring (IFP), and low-frequency preferring (LFP) electrodes.
source: For simplicity, we refer to these groups based on the pulse frequency range at which the maximal intensity occurred: high-frequency preferring (HFP), intermediate-frequency preferring (IFP), and low-frequency preferring (LFP) electrodes.
evidence: This is a description of the naming convention used in the study.

claim: The electrode groups varied in both the median-reported intensity across all frequencies as well as the frequency at which the maximum intensity occurred.
source: These electrode groups varied in both the median-reported intensity across all frequencies as well as the frequency at which the maximum intensity occurred.
evidence: This is a description of the characteristics of the electrode groups identified in the study.

claim: Seven electrodes were tested multiple times (three to six per electrode) to determine whether the relationships between pulse frequency and perceived intensity were consistent across sessions.
source: Seven electrodes were tested multiple times (three to six per electrode) to determine whether the relationships between pulse frequency and perceived intensity were consistent across sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The perceived intensity on these electrodes changed by statistically significant amounts as the stimulus pulse frequency changed (p<0.001, Friedman test).
source: The perceived intensity on these electrodes changed by statistically significant amounts as the stimulus pulse frequency changed (p<0.001, Friedman test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The reported intensities at each frequency on these electrodes did not change significantly across test days (p>0.05, Friedman test).
source: The reported intensities at each frequency on these electrodes did not change significantly across test days (p>0.05, Friedman test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: An additional 22 electrodes were tested in one or two sessions.
source: An additional 22 electrodes were tested in one or two sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Of the 29 electrodes tested in total, 20 electrodes exhibited perceived intensities that changed by statistically significant amounts as the stimulus frequency changed (p<0.02, Friedman test).
source: Of the 29 electrodes tested in total, 20 electrodes exhibited perceived intensities that changed by statistically significant amounts as the stimulus frequency changed (p<0.02, Friedman test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Of the 20 electrodes with significant frequency effects, five were classified as LFP, seven were classified as IFP, and eight were classified as HFP.
source: Of these 20 electrodes, five were classified as LFP, seven were classified as IFP, and eight were classified as HFP.
evidence: This is a summary of the classification results from the study's analysis.

claim: The three different electrode groups had significantly different median intensities (p<0.001, Kruskal–Wallis).
source: The three different electrode groups had significantly different median intensities (p<0.001, Kruskal–Wallis).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Electrodes categorized as IFP had the highest median intensity, while electrodes categorized as HFP had the lowest median intensity.
source: Electrodes categorized as IFP had the highest median intensity, while electrodes categorized as HFP had the lowest median intensity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In participant P3, 23 electrodes were tested at 80 μA and three different frequencies (20, 100, and 300 Hz).
source: In participant P3, we tested 23 electrodes at 80 μA and three different frequencies (20, 100, and 300 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for participant P3.

claim: The perceived intensity changed by statistically significant amounts on 22 electrodes in P3 as the stimulus frequency changed (p<0.05, Friedman test).
source: The perceived intensity changed by statistically significant amounts on 22 electrodes as the stimulus frequency changed (p<0.05, Friedman test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis of participant P3.

claim: In P3, there were similar electrode-specific effects, where some electrodes evoked the highest intensity percepts at the highest frequencies and others had the highest intensity at the lowest frequencies.
source: There were similar electrode-specific effects, where some electrodes evoked the highest intensity percepts at the highest frequencies and others had the highest intensity at the lowest frequencies (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of participant P3, supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Using the same clustering approach in P3, the data divided into two clusters, which were most similar to the LFP and HFP categories.
source: Using the same clustering approach, the data divided into two clusters, which were most similar to the LFP and HFP categories.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of participant P3.

claim: In P3, fifteen electrodes were classified as HFP, and seven were classified as LFP.
source: Fifteen electrodes were classified as HFP, and seven were classified as LFP.
evidence: This is a summary of the classification results for participant P3.

claim: There were no significant differences in the shape of the frequency–intensity relationships for the three electrode groups at 50 and 80 μA after controlling for changes in median intensity caused by increasing current amplitude (p=0.21–0.99, Friedman's test).
source: There were no significant differences in the shape of the frequency–intensity relationships for the three electrode groups at 50 and 80 μA after controlling for changes in median intensity caused by increasing current amplitude (p=0.21–0.99, Friedman's test, Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The reported intensity on LFP electrodes peaked at 20 Hz at both 50 and 80 μA current amplitudes (p=0.02, Kruskal–Wallis).
source: The reported intensity on LFP electrodes peaked at 20 Hz at both current amplitudes (p=0.02, Kruskal–Wallis, Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The reported intensities of IFP electrodes peaked at 100 Hz for both 50 and 80 μA current amplitudes (p<0.001, Kruskal–Wallis).
source: whereas the reported intensities of IFP electrodes peaked at 100 Hz for both current amplitudes (p<0.001, Kruskal–Wallis, Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The reported intensity on HFP electrodes peaked at 300 Hz for both 50 and 80 μA current amplitudes (p<0.001, Kruskal–Wallis).
source: and the reported intensity on HFP electrodes peaked at 300 Hz for both current amplitudes (p<0.001, Kruskal–Wallis, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When the current amplitude was decreased to 20 μA, which was close to the detection threshold for most electrodes, increasing the pulse frequency from 20 to 100 Hz evoked more intense percepts for all electrode groups (p<0.05, Kruskal–Wallis).
source: Interestingly, when we decreased the current amplitude to 20 μA, which was close to the detection threshold for most electrodes, increasing the pulse frequency from 20 to 100 Hz evoked more intense percepts for all electrode groups (p<0.05, Kruskal–Wallis, Figures 2A–C, 20 µA).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, supported by data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: There were highly significant differences between the shape of the frequency–intensity relationships for all groups at 20 μA versus 50 or 80 μA (p<0.001, Friedman's test) even after controlling for changes in the median intensity caused by increasing current amplitude.
source: There were highly significant differences between the shape of the frequency–intensity relationships for all groups at 20 μA versus 50 or 80 μA (p<0.001, Friedman's test) even after controlling for changes in the median intensity caused by increasing current amplitude.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: At 20 μA, the percept intensity was very low, making magnitude estimation akin to a detection task.
source: At 20 μA, the percept intensity was very low, making magnitude estimation akin to a detection task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental conditions at low current amplitudes.

claim: At 300 Hz, the interval containing the stimulus train was correctly identified 80% of the time across all tested electrodes in the detection task.
source: We found that at 300 Hz, the interval containing the stimulus train was correctly identified 80% of the time across all tested electrodes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the detection task experiment, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the pulse frequency was set to 100 Hz, the mean detection accuracy was 72%.
source: Similarly, when the pulse frequency was set to 100 Hz, the mean detection accuracy was 72%.
evidence: This is a finding from the detection task experiment.

claim: When the pulse frequency was set to 20 Hz, the mean detection accuracy was just 42%, which was not significantly different than chance levels of 50% (p=0.14, one-sample t-test).
source: In contrast, when the pulse frequency was set to 20 Hz, the mean detection accuracy was just 42%, which was not significantly different than chance levels of 50% (p=0.14, one-sample t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the detection task experiment.

claim: Detection accuracies at 100 Hz and 300 Hz were significantly higher than the detection accuracy at 20 Hz (p<0.05, ANOVA).
source: Detection accuracies at 100 Hz and 300 Hz were significantly higher than the detection accuracy at 20 Hz (p<0.05, ANOVA) but were not significantly different from each other (p=0.66, ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the detection task experiment.

claim: Detection accuracies at 100 Hz and 300 Hz were not significantly different from each other (p=0.66, ANOVA).
source: Detection accuracies at 100 Hz and 300 Hz were significantly higher than the detection accuracy at 20 Hz (p<0.05, ANOVA) but were not significantly different from each other (p=0.66, ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the detection task experiment.

claim: There were significant differences in the qualities evoked on electrodes belonging to different categories defined by the effect of pulse frequency on intensity in P2.
source: We found that there were significant differences in the qualities evoked on electrodes belonging to different categories defined by the effect of pulse frequency on intensity in P2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The sensory qualities for electrodes in each group were differentially modulated by pulse frequency.
source: Additionally, the sensory qualities for electrodes in each group were differentially modulated by pulse frequency (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 20 Hz, LFP and IFP electrodes evoked percepts with pressure, tapping, sparkle, and touch qualities.
source: At 20 Hz, LFP and IFP electrodes evoked percepts with pressure, tapping, sparkle, and touch qualities.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: These qualities (pressure, tapping, sparkle, and touch) were not evoked on HFP electrodes at any frequency.
source: These qualities were not evoked on HFP electrodes at any frequency.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: At 20 Hz, HFP electrodes were generally not detectable, resulting in few reports of any percepts.
source: At this low stimulation frequency, HFP electrodes were generally not detectable, resulting in few reports of any percepts.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: At 100 Hz, IFP electrodes evoked percepts with buzzing, vibration, and sharp qualities.
source: At 100 Hz, IFP electrodes evoked percepts with buzzing, vibration, and sharp qualities.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: LFP and HFP electrodes never evoked buzzing, vibration, and sharp qualities when stimulated at 100 Hz.
source: LFP and HFP electrodes never evoked these qualities when stimulated at 100 Hz.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: HFP electrodes evoked sensations of touch and prick at 100 Hz that never occurred on LFP or IFP electrodes at any frequency.
source: HFP electrodes also evoked sensations of touch and prick at 100 Hz that never occurred on LFP or IFP electrodes at any frequency.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: Touch and prick qualities occurred on less than 30% of trials on HFP electrodes at 100 Hz.
source: However, these qualities occurred on less than 30% of trials on HFP electrodes.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: At 300 Hz, the responses were similar to those at 100 Hz except that all electrode categories evoked less pressure.
source: At 300 Hz, the responses were similar to those at 100 Hz except that all electrode categories evoked less pressure.
evidence: This is a finding from the quality analysis.

claim: Electrode clusters based on verbal reports of percept quality at all frequencies were remarkably similar to those based on intensity responses at different frequencies.
source: Interestingly, these clusters were remarkably similar to those based on intensity responses at different frequencies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was significant clustering of electrodes in the same category across arrays in P2 (pseudo-p=0.00017).
source: In P2, there was significant clustering of electrodes in the same category (Figure 4A) across arrays (pseudo-p=0.00017).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the spatial analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In P3, LFP electrodes only occurred on one of the arrays, which resulted in clustering across the arrays (pseudo-p=0.0045, LISA).
source: In P3, LFP electrodes only occurred on one of the arrays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which resulted in clustering across the arrays (pseudo-p=0.0045, local indicators of spatial association [LISA]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the spatial analysis of participant P3, supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intracortical microstimulation at the maximum amplitudes used in this study can directly activate neurons up to 2 mm away from the electrode tip.
source: Intracortical microstimulation at the maximum amplitudes used in this study can directly activate neurons up to 2 mm away from the electrode tip, but most activation occurs less than 500 µm from the electrode tip (Overstreet et al., 2013; Stoney et al., 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on ICMS activation.

claim: Most activation from ICMS occurs less than 500 µm from the electrode tip.
source: Intracortical microstimulation at the maximum amplitudes used in this study can directly activate neurons up to 2 mm away from the electrode tip, but most activation occurs less than 500 µm from the electrode tip (Overstreet et al., 2013; Stoney et al., 1968).
